# North Pacific Strategy Initiative — full machine-readable index

> An independent research imprint publishing reference-grade working papers on Pacific sovereignty, bilateral financial architecture, and the defensive options available to middle powers in a period of dollar-system stress. Edited in Victoria, British Columbia. Working-paper text is licensed CC-BY-4.0; the imprint and wordmark are not licensed.

This file is the full-content companion to https://npsi.ca/llms.txt. It carries
the complete abstract, key findings, and citation metadata for every document
the imprint has published. Index last revised 17 October 2026; status lines
describe each document as at its release unless dated otherwise.

How to cite: James, J. ([Year]). *[Title]* (NPSI Working Paper No. [N],
v[M.m]). North Pacific Strategy Initiative. https://npsi.ca/wp[N]/. Substitute
Technical Briefing / Briefing Note / Special Briefing and the matching URL for
the other series. Document IDs follow NPSI-WP-NNN (working papers), NPSI-TB-NNN
(technical briefings), NPSI-BN-NNN (briefing notes), NPSI-SB-NNN (special
briefings), NPSI-PL-NNN (The Pacific Ledger, the Canada–Korea account); Special
Briefings Nos. 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9, Technical Briefing No. 2 and Ledger №02 keep
the date-based IDs printed on their releases (NPSI-20261003-B, NPSI-20261003-C,
NPSI-20261002-A, NPSI-20260920-B, NPSI-20261016, NPSI-20261014, NPSI-20261001-A), accession
numbers whose publication serials are pending. Every document has an HTML page at its
canonical URL with Highwire citation_* meta tags and Schema.org JSON-LD. For
PDF-first releases (WP5, WP10, WP11, SB2, SB3, SB4, SB5) the PDF is the
canonical release document; WP10 and SB3 have release pages rather than full
reading views; SB4 and SB5 carry full reading views ported from their corrected
releases on 14 October 2026. Editor: Jesse James
(editor@npsi.ca). Numbering is the author's: WP6 and WP8 are unreleased, so the
archive carries intentional gaps at 6 and 8.

## Working Paper No. 11 — Rated AAA by the Issuer

- ID: NPSI-WP-011 · Technical Series · v1.0.1 (reading view; PDF v1.0) · 28 July 2026 · errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp11/ · PDF (18 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp11/working-paper.pdf
- Status: the current working paper. Supersedes WP10, which remains available unaltered with a correction notice.
- Keywords: open source AI, credit ratings, quality labels, base rates, forecasting, OSAID, EU AI Act, open weights, certification, capability thresholds

Abstract: There is no enforced definition of open source in artificial
intelligence. A standards body wrote one and cannot compel anyone to use it; a
regulator wrote a different one that binds in a single jurisdiction; a
procurement authority asked departments to consider the thing and never defined it
at all. In that vacuum, the company that builds a model is the party that
declares it open — the labeller is the labelled. The closest precedent is not
open-source software but the credit rating. The paper corrects its predecessor
(WP-10) in a published correction notice, establishes that the July 2026 policy
fight is not about whether to ban open-weight models but about who defines
"sufficiently capable," and applies documented base rates from four other
markets that ran unenforced quality labels to produce a forecast, with
probabilities, of how this one resolves.

Key findings: Three standing corrections to WP10 are published at §1 (a fourth, on sourcing, was withdrawn by erratum on 14 October 2026; the first is under review against the court's final order), including
the framing correction that Anthropic is the most restriction-friendly major
lab on open weights and has not called for a ban — both halves true. Both camps
in the July 2026 fight (the 24 July Nvidia-hosted multi-signatory letter and
Anthropic) reject a categorical ban in writing; the live leverage is in who
defines the capability threshold, which falls disproportionately on open
releases because guardrails cannot be reimposed after weights ship. The
base-rate table covers four label markets — organic (resolved by statute after
~12 years), Energy Star (certifier hardening after GAO-10-470), credit ratings
(statute after systemic failure), and "natural" (never resolved) — and the §5
forecast assigns probabilities with named falsifiers: label decays 45%,
certifier gets teeth 20%, capability capture 25%, certifier captured 10%.
Author's disclosure: drafted with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), whose
statements the paper examines.

## Working Paper No. 9 — The Counterparty Problem

- ID: NPSI-WP-009 · v1.0.1 · 27 July 2026 · errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp9/ · PDF (12 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp9/working-paper.pdf
- Companions: WP1 (counterparty-diversification thesis), SB2 (the EXIM SCRI door)
- Keywords: export credit, EXIM, Memorandum of Understanding, treaty withdrawal, commitment reliability, counterparty risk, sovereign wealth funds, reauthorization, Congress, Public Investment Fund

Abstract: U.S. reliability is not one question but two, and conflating them
produces bad risk analysis. The United States has a real, documented and
recently accelerating record of formally exiting binding treaties — roughly
fifteen significant withdrawals or repudiations since 2001 — but no honest
failure-to-convert base rate can be computed for non-binding instruments like
MoUs, because no registry of U.S. MoUs exists. The paper assesses the
24 July 2026 PIF–EXIM $15 billion MoU against the sharpest available case
study: EXIM's 2015–2019 board-quorum lapse, which cut the bank's financing by
almost 85 percent, and a charter that expires again on 31 December 2026 with
reauthorization still in committee (as of 27 July 2026).

Key findings: Formal withdrawals cluster in 2017–2020 and 2025–2026. The
PIF–EXIM instrument is explicitly non-binding; EXIM's charter expires
31 December 2026, with the Senate's ten-year extension bill in committee and no
markup (as of 27 July 2026). During the 2015–2019 quorum lapse, financing declined roughly 85
percent, and each dollar of EXIM financing supports approximately $4.50 of
exports. The paper's balance is load-bearing: it concedes democratic policy
alternation, the honoured-commitment record (NATO Article 5, Bretton Woods, the
Japan and Korea treaties), and that other states have worse records. The
framing is counterparty-risk pricing, not anti-American critique.

## Working Paper No. 10 — Fair Use for We, IP Theft for Thee

- ID: NPSI-WP-010 · Technical Series · v1.0 · 26 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp10/ · PDF (17 pp., canonical): https://npsi.ca/wp10/working-paper.pdf
- Status: superseded by WP11 (corrections itemised at its §1); remains available unaltered with a correction notice attached.
- Keywords: open source AI, OSAID, open weights, model licences, Llama, EU AI Act, fair use, distillation, copyright litigation, procurement, Canada

Abstract: Between 16 and 24 July 2026 the United States government came closer
to restricting foreign open-weight AI models than at any point in the
technology's existence — and not one of the statements driving that policy
rests on an agreed definition of the thing being restricted. The paper reads
the licences: of eleven major model families surveyed, three satisfy the Open
Source Initiative's definition, and none of those three operates at frontier
scale. Llama 4's licence withholds rights from anyone domiciled in the European
Union, inside a product marketed as open source, in the one jurisdiction that
offers open-source models a regulatory exemption. And the characterisation now
driving policy — that training on another party's output is fair use when
American labs do it and theft when Chinese labs do it — is real at the level of
framing, weaker than advertised at the level of evidence, and applied to
conduct that three separate bodies of law treat three separate ways.

Key findings: OSAID v1.0 (October 2024) has been adopted as a binding criterion
by no regulator or procurement authority located in the survey; of eleven model
families, three meet the definition (OLMo 2, Pythia/GPT-NeoX, arguably BLOOM),
none at frontier scale. The paper's spine is a three-category legal separation:
taking model weights is theft, uncontested; training on scraped outputs is
contested and litigated; acquiring pirated corpora has been adjudicated against
the lab (the Bartz v. Anthropic settlement). Every claim is evidence-graded
VERIFIED / CORROBORATED / ATTRIBUTED / UNDETERMINED. Author's disclosure:
drafted with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), whose conduct §6 examines.
Read with WP11's correction notice.

## Working Paper No. 7 — Dazzle 2.0

- ID: NPSI-WP-007 · Counter-Autonomy Series (first paper) · v1.0.1 · 12 July 2026 · errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp7/ · PDF (11 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp7/working-paper.pdf
- Companion: TB1 — The Verified Sky (the sensing substrate)
- Keywords: adversarial machine learning, dazzle camouflage, machine vision, drones, counter-autonomy, loitering munitions, sensor fusion, procurement, NATO, Canada

Abstract: Russian logistics trucks in Ukraine have worn high-contrast dazzle
paint since late May 2026, and the intent — degrading the machine vision on
strike drones — is accepted by serious analysts. But no controlled test shows
the tactic defeating any named detector. The durable finding is cost asymmetry:
a paint can iterates in an afternoon; a fielded detector re-learns only as fast
as its slowest update loop. The paper separates confirmed fact from inference
and hype, and draws the procurement lesson for NATO and Canada: vision-only
terminal guidance is brittle; sensor fusion, human authorization, and
edge-retrainable models are the robust answers.

Key findings: Every load-bearing claim is tagged Confirmed / Plausible /
Speculation / Hype in the §2 evidence table. The most plausible mechanism is
out-of-distribution confusion, not an engineered adversarial attack; three gaps
(optimization, physical robustness, transferability) separate crude stripes
from the academically proven ceiling (Eykholt et al. CVPR 2018; adversarial
patches; CAMOU-class vehicle textures). The durable finding is cost asymmetry,
anchored to the CENTCOM aircraft-tire case where the retraining loop ran up to
six months. Five procurement recommendations: multi-sensor seekers,
human-on-the-loop authorization, edge-retrainable models with organic
labeling, adversarial and out-of-distribution inputs in acceptance testing, and
no single-vendor black-box automatic target recognition.

## Working Paper No. 5 — Sovereign Compute North

- ID: NPSI-WP-005 · v1.0.1 (reading view; PDF v1.0) · 27 May 2026 · errata 14 October 2026 · Co-issued with Fit For Gov
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp5/ · PDF (19 pp., canonical): https://npsi.ca/wp5/working-paper.pdf
- Companion: SB1 — Zero Secrets (the exposure audit)
- Keywords: data sovereignty, sovereign cloud, Canada, Korea, HBM, hydroelectricity, data centres, CLOUD Act, sovereign compute, municipal infrastructure

Abstract: Canada has the cheapest low-carbon firm electricity in the G7. Korea
controls the global memory chokepoint on which every modern AI accelerator
depends. Microsoft France has stated under oath (French Senate, 10 June 2025)
that it cannot guarantee French citizens' data against US extraterritorial
reach. The trade is obvious: Canadian electrons, Korean
memory, Canadian law, Korean and allied capital — combined into a
government-owned compute fabric that reaches from the Hydro-Québec switchyard
to the municipal town hall.

Key findings: An energy-for-memory swap signed under Canadian law — a
government-owned, allies-financed, Canadian-law-bound compute fabric anchored
on surplus Canadian power and Korea-led sovereign capital, extended to the
municipal layer. The paper specifies the control-based sovereignty test
(jurisdictional, operational, cryptographic, audit), the five Canadian Digital
Sovereignty Standard clauses, the provincial power inventory, and the capital
stack. Sits inside the three-rail Pacific architecture with WP1 (financial
rail) and WP2 (energy/compute rail).

## Working Paper No. 4 — The Addition Paradox

- ID: NPSI-WP-004 · v1.0.1 · 15 May 2026 · errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp4/ · PDF (9 pp., printed from the reading view): https://npsi.ca/wp4/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, energy transition, oil sands, hydroelectricity, uranium, critical minerals, clean-energy concentration, Pacific export capacity

Abstract: Why the energy transition did not happen, why that is acceptable, and
why Canada is uniquely positioned to win the forty years that follow. A record
year for clean-energy deployment was also a record year for fossil combustion:
the global system did not transition, it expanded.

Key findings: 2024 saw a record 858 TWh of new clean electricity and record
fossil combustion; global electricity demand grew 1,172 TWh, so fossil supplied
the remaining 314 TWh; coal remains the largest single source into the
mid-2030s. Chokepoint risk migrated from molecules to minerals: clean-tech
refining and assembly concentrate in a single nation (polysilicon ≈95%, lithium
cells ≈80%, NdFeB magnets ≈90%) — framed as concentration risk, not as an
argument against clean energy. Canada holds four assets on one hand: the
third-largest oil reserves with a barrel among the cleanest of any major
producer, the largest per-capita clean electricity in the G7, the
second-largest reserves of high-grade uranium (Athabasca Basin), and Pacific
and Atlantic deepwater export capacity — a combination no other G7 nation
holds.
Strategic preface to the three-rail architecture (WP1, WP2, WP3).

## Working Paper No. 3 — A Canada–Korea Pacific Defence-Industrial Corridor

- ID: NPSI-WP-003 · v1.0.2 · first published May 2026; revised 29 July 2026 and 14 October 2026 (errata; editor's note on the 6 July 2026 CPSP decision — TKMS preferred supplier, Hanwha Ocean reserve)
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp3/ · PDF (32 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp3/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, Korea, CPSP, submarines, KSS-III, Hanwha, defence-industrial, bilateral defence cooperation, CKFTA, SDCP

Abstract: A bilateral defence-industrial architecture pairing the Canadian
Patrol Submarine Project with the Hanwha–Algoma Steel and Hanwha–APMA
industrial-offset structures, anchored to the CKFTA institutional foundation,
the October 2025 SDCP, and the 25 February 2026 Foreign and Defence (2+2)
Ministerial Joint Statement.

Key findings: The Canadian Patrol Submarine Project (up to 12 boats by 2035;
Hanwha Ocean and TKMS confirmed as the two qualified suppliers, 19 August 2025)
read against Korea's offset posture: the binding but conditional Hanwha–Algoma MOU (26 January 2026; suspended by
Algoma 29 July 2026) and the conditional Hanwha–APMA MOU (29 April 2026), with the
30 October 2025 Carney–Lee Security and Defence Cooperation Partnership as the
institutional anchor. Completes the three-rail Pacific architecture as the
defence-industrial rail alongside WP1 (financial) and WP2 (energy/compute).

## Working Paper No. 2 — A Canada–United States Energy and Compute Compact

- ID: NPSI-WP-002 · v1.0.1 · May 2026; errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp2/ · PDF (46 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp2/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, United States, CUSMA, AI compute, hydroelectricity, ultra-high-voltage transmission, bilateral compact

Abstract: A treaty-grade bilateral architecture pairing Canadian dispatchable
generation with the U.S. grid through ultra-high-voltage transmission, siting
AI training workloads on Canadian hydro-electric capacity, and preserving
inference workloads at the U.S. urban edge. Structurally complementary to
Working Paper No. 1; financed through the same supranational vehicle.

Key findings: The U.S. faces a structural capacity gap (~44 GW required by 2028
against ~25 GW deliverable, the paper's own derivation from the LBNL 2028
demand range); combined dispatchable Canadian hydro is
approximately 56,000 MW across Hydro-Québec, BC Hydro, and Manitoba Hydro. AI
workloads bifurcate — training is latency-agnostic and can sit on Canadian
hydro, inference stays at the U.S. urban edge — and inference, roughly at parity
with training today, reaches about 60 percent of AI compute capacity by 2030
(~22% against ~35% CAGR). Three corridor candidates
(Saguenay/Côte-Nord, Peace River/Bennett, Northern Manitoba), an Indigenous
Series II tranche of 10–15 percent of compact capex, and survival independent
of CUSMA renewal.

## Working Paper No. 1 — The Bilateral Foundation

- ID: NPSI-WP-001 · v1.0.1 · May 2026 (technical specification, April 2026 — the reading view; essay edition PDF, 15 May 2026); errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical (technical specification): https://npsi.ca/wp1/ · PDF (essay edition, 15 May 2026, 17 pp., stands as issued with its errata declared on the page): https://npsi.ca/wp1/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, Korea, sovereign bonds, CKPIF, Pacific architecture, bilateral finance, middle-power policy

Abstract: A thirty-year Canada–Korea co-issued sovereign infrastructure bond —
assembled from off-the-shelf instruments, priced as a spread over US
Treasuries, with Indigenous co-ownership embedded at issuance — as the
architecture of middle-power independence.

Key findings: Proposes the Canada–Korea Pacific Infrastructure Facility
(CKPIF): a treaty-based supranational issuer with 50/50 ownership, Luxembourg
seat, English law, and LCIA arbitration; indicative programme size US$25–40
billion over 5–7 years, priced indicatively +50–80 bp over 30-year US
Treasuries; several (not joint) sovereign guarantees. An Indigenous Series I
tranche of 10–15 percent of programme with +25 bp ratchet protection; KPI
architecture on ICMA Sustainability-Linked Bond Principles; a tokenised pilot
tranche of US$200–500 million on Project Agorá-class infrastructure. The
institutional foundation is the Bank of Canada–Bank of Korea standing swap
line, signed November 2017, with no expiry and no preset limit.

## The Pacific Ledger — №02 · October 2026

- ID: NPSI-20261001-A (accession number; publication serial pending) · The Pacific Ledger · issue closed 1 October 2026; published 14 October 2026 with pre-publication corrections applied
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/pl2/ · PDF (10 pp., printed from the reading view): https://npsi.ca/pl2/pacific-ledger.pdf
- Series: The Pacific Ledger is the imprint's account of the Canada–Korea relationship — every entry sourced, both sides recorded. Issues close when the account warrants one (№01 closed 28 July 2026; №02 closed 1 October 2026).
- Keywords: Canada, Korea, foreign direct investment, Canadian Patrol Submarine Project, Hanwha Ocean, TKMS, Project Beaver, Algoma Steel, NextStar Energy, Ultium CAM, LNG Canada, CUSMA, Pacific

Abstract: The second issue carries one entry: the editor's sorting of every
Korean commitment made around the Canadian Patrol Submarine Project after
Ottawa named TKMS preferred supplier on 6 July 2026 and designated Hanwha
Ocean reserve supplier. Thirteen commitments are tiered by condition: five
contingent on a Hanwha Ocean award, which have lapsed, been suspended,
shelved or sit under review; five bid-linked with no stated condition, which
continue as research, trade and intent; and three independent of the bid,
the only ones with capital in the ground. NextStar in Windsor and KOGAS's
5 percent stake in LNG Canada are operating; Ultium CAM in Bécancour is
scheduled to start production in late October 2026.

Key entries: The Korean bid, led by Hanwha Ocean with HD Hyundai Heavy
Industries, carried a headline of more than C$70 billion in trade and
investment (Globe and Mail, 6 July); DAPA said within three weeks that its
pledge was conditional from the outset. Contingent: DAPA package (lapsed);
Hanwha Ocean–Algoma binding MOU of 26 January 2026, up to US$250M (about
C$345M at signing), suspended by Algoma on 29 July 2026 "unless and until
Hanwha Ocean is selected"; Project Beaver, more than C$3.1B and about 9,000
jobs from 2030, under review per Hyundai (23 July) after a reported
withdrawal (9 July); Hanwha–APMA military-vehicle joint venture, shelved;
Hanwha Ocean–Ontario Shipyards–Mohawk College training hub, stopped.
Bid-linked, continuing: LIG D&A (formerly LIG Nex1); HD Hyundai Oilbank crude
("trillions of won over the programme"); HD KSOE research MOU with UBC (8 June
2026); Cohere's AI collaboration with Hanwha; the envoy's energy expansion
pitch (LNG Canada stake from about C$1.6B to C$3.2B; 16M barrels of crude in
2026, up to 20M in 2027). Independent: NextStar (more than C$5B; cells since
November 2025; Stellantis's 49 percent sold for a nominal US$100, closed
31 March 2026 per Stellantis's SEC filings); Ultium CAM (POSCO Future M 85
percent; phase 1 about C$600M; phase 2 on hold indefinitely); KOGAS in LNG
Canada. Watch: record conditionality as a field; keep metric types apart
(C$70B trade and investment, >C$120B GDP, C$167B economic activity are not
FDI); treat contingent pledges as dormant, not dead (Ottawa contracts by
end-2027 and may designate Hanwha Ocean if talks fail); convert what survives
through the January 2026 Canada–Korea Industrial Cooperation Committee, with
the Productivity Mega Deduction announced 15 September 2026 improving the
standalone arithmetic. Interest note on the three energy entries; AI
assistance (Claude) stated; open items published (Beaver's status, Ultium
CAM's start, cathode material under the 22 August US duties).

## The Pacific Ledger — №01 · July 2026 (Premier Issue)

- ID: NPSI-PL-001 · The Pacific Ledger · issue closed 28 July 2026 · v1.0.1, corrected 14 October 2026 (author PDF of 28 July stands as issued)
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/pl1/ · PDF (7 pp.): https://npsi.ca/pl1/pacific-ledger.pdf
- Series: The Pacific Ledger is the imprint's account of the Canada–Korea relationship — every entry sourced, both sides recorded. Issues close when the account warrants one. Document IDs follow NPSI-PL-NNN.
- Keywords: Canada, Korea, trade, LNG, crude oil, batteries, critical minerals, submarine procurement, CKFTA, Kapyong, Pacific

Abstract: The Canada–Korea account. Premier issue: on
July 6 Canada named TKMS preferred supplier for the Canadian Patrol Submarine
Project over Hanwha's KSS-III — and the relationship spent the rest of the
month posting new entries anyway. The ledger records LNG Canada's first cargo
into KOGAS's Incheon terminal (Kitimat May 20 → Incheon June 3), a planned rise
of up to 3.3× in Canadian crude to Korea, LG Energy Solution's buyout of the
NextStar battery plant (agreed 6 February, closed 31 March 2026), a joint
critical-minerals stockpiling plan due end-2026, fifty years of CANDU–KHNP
collaboration, Defence Cooperation Agreement negotiations launched at the
June 16 G7 bilateral, and Kapyong at 75.

Key entries: Two-way merchandise trade C$25 billion in 2025; Korea is Canada's
seventh-largest trading partner; Korean direct investment stock in Canada
C$17.6 billion at end-2025 by ultimate investor (C$14.4 billion by immediate
investor); 99 percent of Canadian exports to Korea eligible for duty-free
access under CKFTA. Korea's Middle East LNG dependence fell from 45
percent (2022) to 24 percent (2025), with a KOGAS target of 18 percent or less for 2026; "not a
single Korean LNG carrier is trapped inside the Strait of Hormuz" (KOGAS CEO
Choi Yeon-hye, June 5). Canadian crude to Korea expands from 4.88
million barrels (2025) to as much as 16 million (2026) — at that volume Korea
would become the third-largest buyer after the U.S. and China. Debit column recorded honestly: Hanwha's contingent
armoured-vehicle JV and DAPA equity stake shelved; Hyundai's Project Beaver
carried as unresolved. Open items published: the Korean masthead subtitle is
pending native-speaker review; the late-July DPRK troop-deployment figure is a
claim, not a confirmation.

## Technical Briefing No. 2 — Running Silent

- ID: NPSI-20261014 (accession number; publication serial pending) · v1.0.1 · dated 14 October 2026; published 17 October 2026 and corrected the same day
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/tb2/ (reading view, set from the author's Markdown record) · PDF (23 pp., dark edition, reissued at v1.0.1): https://npsi.ca/tb2/technical-briefing.pdf · print edition (23 pp., cream): https://npsi.ca/tb2/technical-briefing-print.pdf
- Keywords: over-the-horizon targeting, passive radar, VLF, skin depth, submarine detection, magnetic anomaly detection, undersea surveillance, distributed acoustic sensing, AIS, dark vessels, GNSS spoofing, sensor fusion, Maven Smart System, emission control, cognitive electronic warfare
- Notes: grades every claim (a) established, (b) demonstrated, (c) speculative or (d) wrong; eighteen claims in a verification ledger, ten figures, nine chapters, sources grouped by chapter. Carries an interest note (the editor's enterprise-software and applied-intelligence work; https://npsi.ca/disclosure/) and states its AI drafting assistance. v1.0.1 corrects the hull-to-wavelength ratio and Rayleigh estimate, the depth at which seawater ends the VLF story, the Paolo et al. quotation (vessel activity), the Hensoldt and Diehl passive-radar figures, the Feinberg memo, the G-Cloud 14 description of Gaia, and several attributions; drops a withdrawn preprint; and links the sources. Classified capability is neither claimed nor assessed.

Abstract: A claim-by-claim technical assessment of a widely circulated
AI-generated text claiming that ambient radio, commercial transponder feeds and
machine learning can be fused into a real-time global map of hidden submarines
and carrier groups. Multi-sensor fusion is eroding concealment at sea, but the
three mechanisms the text relies on fail: seawater extinguishes a VLF field
within metres, a ship that is not broadcasting is absent from an AIS feed
rather than revealed by subtracting it, and no published mechanism turns
micro-variance in background satellite signal strength into a carrier track.
What works is narrower, more expensive and more active: satellite radar matched
against AIS, satellite geolocation of ships that still emit, seabed and towed
acoustic arrays, skywave over-the-horizon radar cued to imaging satellites, and
fusion software at scale. None of it makes running silent obsolete; it makes
running silent insufficient on its own.

Key findings: Eighteen claims graded: five established, one demonstrated, seven
speculative, four wrong as written and one between speculative and wrong.
Seawater's skin depth at 20 kHz is about 1.8 m, so a submarine at 100 m sits
nearly 490 dB below the surface field. Radar matched to AIS finds that 72–76%
of the world's industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked (Paolo et
al., Nature, 2024). Satellite-illuminated passive radar reaches kilometres, not
oceans. The real over-the-horizon chain against carriers is active and
dedicated, skywave radar cued to imaging and electronic-intelligence
satellites, and is not documented as tested end to end against a defended,
manoeuvring carrier. Fusion at scale is real: the Maven Smart System ceiling is
about $1.3 billion through 2029, with more than 100,000 US users by September
2026; Palantir's Gaia is a map application, not a sensor. Emission control,
dispersion and deception still impose large search costs; running silent alone
is increasingly insufficient against a peer with proliferated space
surveillance.

## Technical Briefing No. 1 — The Verified Sky

- ID: NPSI-TB-001 · v1.0.1 · 11 June 2026 · errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/tb1/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/tb1/technical-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: airspace awareness, computer vision, sensor fusion, counter-UAS, Remote ID, verification architecture, edge AI, Canada, Radiocommunication Act, PIPEDA

Abstract: A survey of the 2025–2026 state of the art in computer vision and
sensing for monitoring a defined volume of airspace; the verification
architecture that converts a probabilistic detection into a near-certain
identification; realistic detection-to-action latency; the statutory line
between lawful and criminal automated response for a private Canadian operator;
and a deliberately conservative capability forecast at one, two-and-a-half, and
five years.

Key findings: The signature element is the verification ledger — seven
conditions (class, size, altitude, kinematics, window, geofence, persistence)
that must all pass before any action fires, with two-sensor corroboration as
the standing industry rule. Benchmark honesty: realistic small-and-distant
detection performance runs at roughly half of headline benchmark performance.
The Canadian legal line: detection, tracking, evidence, and notification are
lawful for civil operators; jamming, spoofing, takeover, and physical downing
are not. Explicitly a technical and regulatory survey, not legal advice.

## Briefing Note No. 1 — The Voter File

- ID: NPSI-BN-001 · v1.0.1 · 11 June 2026 · errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/bn1/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/bn1/briefing-note.pdf
- Keywords: voter files, political parties, privacy law, Canada Elections Act, Bill C-4, PIPEDA, data-driven campaigning, microtargeting

Abstract: Every major Canadian federal political party maintains a database
with a record on substantially every voter, assembled in five layers: the
Elections Canada list of electors, canvassing observations, appended public
records, appended commercial data, and modelled behavioural scores. No layer
requires consent; no layer grants a right of access. In March 2026, Part 4 of
Bill C-4 excluded federal parties from provincial and territorial privacy law,
retroactive to 2000.

Key findings: The five-layer file documented end to end, with the legal
chronology: PIPEDA never applied; Bill C-76 (2018) required only a published
privacy policy; BC OIPC Order P22-02 (2022) and the 2024 BC Supreme Court
judicial review found BC PIPA could apply; Bill C-4 Part 4 (S.C. 2026, c. 2;
royal assent 12 March 2026) excluded federal parties from provincial and
territorial privacy law retroactive to 2000, leaving voters no right of access
or correction, with the Senate's three-year
sunset amendment rejected. Explicitly non-partisan; the illustrative voter
record is fictional and labelled as such.

## Special Briefing No. 9 — Settled in Cash

- ID: NPSI-20261016 (accession number; publication serial pending) · v1.0 · dated 16 October 2026; published 17 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb9/ (reading view, set from the author's HTML) · PDF (11 pp.): https://npsi.ca/sb9/special-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: AI infrastructure, data centres, power delivery, CoreWeave, credit, gold, COMEX, futures, Treasury market, Federal Reserve, passive investing, ERCOT, Dominion Energy, PJM, KOSPI
- Notes: a signed briefing in the first person; six figures; a fifteen-claim verification ledger; sources grouped and linked. Carries an interest note for the editor's declared energy-sector work and the adjacent applied-intelligence work, and states its AI drafting assistance (https://npsi.ca/disclosure/). Released with pre-publication corrections applied, listed at the foot of the page. No. 7 in this line remains reserved.

Abstract: The AI build was priced like a futures contract. A data centre only
settles one way: physical delivery of power. In mid-October 2026 the S&P 500
sat less than 1% below its record while the assets closest to the data centre
fell hardest: Korea's KOSPI lost 7.57% in a session and CoreWeave's 9% notes
traded at 80.75, a yield near 15.3%. Dominion Energy has about 54 GW of
data-centre capacity under contract against a 4.8 GW data-centre billing peak; gold's paper on COMEX runs
about 2.7 times registered metal. Gold, crude, the October credit scare and the
money loop are checked against the record, claim by claim.

Key findings: The S&P 500 closed 15 October 0.96% below its 6 October record;
the assets closest to the data centre fell hardest (KOSPI −7.57% in a session;
CoreWeave's 9% notes due 2031 at 80.75, default insurance past 1,000 bp). Claims
run ahead of delivery: COMEX open interest about 2.7 times registered gold,
Dominion about 54 GW of data-centre capacity contracted against a 4.8 GW
data-centre billing peak, Texas about 474 GW seeking to connect against a 91 GW
record peak. Gold at $4,147 on 15 October sat 26% below its January record and 3 to 4%
below its level a month earlier; the larger flight to quality went into
Treasuries. Exposure is structural: the ten largest stocks are about 38% of the
S&P 500 and index funds hold about 54% of US long-term mutual fund and ETF
assets.

## Special Briefing No. 8 — The Authored State

- ID: NPSI-20260920-B (accession number; serial pending the editor's ruling) · v1.0 · dated 19 September 2026; released 14 October 2026 with pre-publication corrections applied
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb8/ (reading view) · PDF (43 pp., printed from the reading view): https://npsi.ca/sb8/special-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: authored institutions, consociationalism, Lebanon, Iraq, Bosnia, Northern Ireland, Cyprus, Rwanda, France, nuclear fuel cycle, Rosatom, Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb, Indus Waters Treaty, Radcliffe Line, Social Security, reserve currency, inflation targeting
- Notes: a signed briefing written in the first person, with judgements marked as the author's; carries an interest note for the editor's declared energy-sector work (https://npsi.ca/disclosure/) and states its AI drafting assistance in the metadata block. Four inline figures (a table of the six settlements and two controls; IEA's August 2026 Hormuz count; France's "Unspecified" uranium line 2019–2024; VLCC earnings, September 2026). The page lists the corrections applied before release and the claims not re-verified. No. 7 in this line is reserved for a document whose source has not arrived.

Abstract: An outside power writes the rules by which a country governs
itself and goes home; the formula hardens because a local class finds that
the broken system guarantees its position. The evidence is set out as
testimony in seven exhibits: Lebanon's 1932 census and its banks; Iraq,
Bosnia, Northern Ireland, Cyprus and Rwanda; France audited as an author,
from its nuclear fuel cycle to its pensions; three of the author's claims
withdrawn; Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb in 2026; Radcliffe's line and the Indus;
and the reader's own inflation target, pension and reserve currency. The
finding is narrow: fix identity into the distribution of power and you
manufacture a class that defends the formula after it has stopped defending
anyone else.

Key findings: Lebanon has not counted itself since 1932; the 1926
constitution came first and the census supplied the ratios; financial losses
exceed $72 billion, more than three times 2021 GDP, and were never allocated;
the central bank holds about $11.7 billion in foreign currency against a
draft law that would repay $22 billion to small depositors. Iraq, Bosnia,
Northern Ireland, Cyprus and Rwanda had identity written into their rules by
an outside author (fixed ratios, ethnic offices, an unwritten quota, a
community designation, a card); Iraq took 382 days to form a government in
2022 and Northern Ireland's Executive had spent 41.5 percent of its
existence collapsed by July 2023; Germany and Japan, the controls, count
citizens. France's reprocessed uranium is re-enriched at scale only at
Seversk; the EU left nuclear fuel out of sanctions with French support;
Russia supplied 26 to 31 percent of EU utilities' enrichment services in
2020–22. Three of the author's claims are withdrawn: there was no 1974
petrodollar treaty; the IEA puts Gulf output shut in near 10 million barrels
a day, with Hormuz flows at 7.6 million in August 2026; France's
"Unspecified" uranium import line existed from 2020. Houthi forces took
Mocha and Perim Island on 10–11 September 2026, and the Baltic Exchange's
VLCC Gulf-to-China assessment reached $1.21 million a day on 17 September.

## Special Briefing No. 6 — The Walk-Away Price

- ID: NPSI-20261002-A (accession number; publication serial pending) · v1.0 · assessment dated 2 October 2026; published 14 October 2026 with pre-publication corrections applied
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb6/ (reading view) · PDF (27 pp., printed from the reading view): https://npsi.ca/sb6/special-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: Korea, United States, Strategic Investment MOU, Alaska LNG, refusal right, Special Act, IEEPA, Section 301, Section 232, tariffs, Hormuz, 123 Agreement
- Notes: written in the author's voice, with recommendations addressed to Korea's Consultation Committee; carries a declared-interests note (the editor's work for an international energy facilitation firm, Korea Pro's paid commission of July 2026, AI drafting assistance; https://npsi.ca/disclosure/). The page carries eight sections, six figures (one table, five SVG), a dated postscript on the President's remarks of 2 October, 63 numbered sources, and a note listing what the pre-publication source check corrected. The text speaks as of 2 October 2026.

Abstract: Korea wired the first $2.4 billion of its $200 billion US
strategic-investment commitment on 1 October 2026 and, the same day, protested
the way Washington had announced the Alaska LNG project. It reads both against
the texts: the Strategic Investment MOU, whose written price of refusal, a
diversion of Korea's returns equal to the unfunded amount plus a tariff remedy,
is rarely quoted whole; the $20 billion annual cap; Korea's Special Act; and
the Supreme Court's February ruling, which moved any tariff penalty to a
Section 301 docket or the Section 232 auto rate. It prices a first refusal on
Alaska and names the disbursement, the reactor advance of up to $10 billion,
where Seoul's refusal buys something money cannot.

Key findings: The MOU's refusal right (¶9) is written down and real, but the
MOU itself creates no legally binding rights (¶25); what binds Seoul is its
own Special Act of 12 March 2026, and the operating agreement that would make
the $20 billion annual cap and the $200 billion total binding was agreed on
1 October, not signed. The written price of refusal has two parts: Korea's
returns on funded projects are diverted until Washington has recovered a sum
equal to the unfunded amount, and the United States "may also" impose tariffs
at a rate determined by the President with no stated ceiling; Japan's MOU of
4 September 2025 (¶8) carries the identical clause, and what Japan lacks is
the cap, the commercial-reasonableness test and a Korean-chaired Consultation
Committee. After Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (20 February 2026, 6–3,
IEEPA does not authorise tariffs), a penalty must travel through a Section 301
docket, slower and reviewable, or the Section 232 auto rate (15 percent from
1 November 2025), which the ruling left alone; only the reciprocal part of the
26 January 25-percent threat ran on IEEPA and it was never given effect.
Alaska LNG is the first test of the clause: Lutnick's "just over $50 billion"
against $57.7 billion of room if the nuclear framework (up to $120 billion) is
drawn in full and a Glenfarne whole-project estimate of $44.5–54.5 billion;
Glenfarne holds 13 of the 16 million tonnes a year it needs under preliminary
agreements, and KOGAS is not among the buyers. A ten-point tariff rise on
$122.9 billion of 2025 exports is about $12 billion a year gross, about $49
billion over four years, a static illustration rather than a forecast. The
moment to spend the refusal is the advance of up to $10 billion for reactor
components the two sides agreed to work toward before year-end, set against
the undated second round of 123 Agreement talks. Postscript: on 2 October, US
time, the President said "I'll just charge them more" and "double it up", and
posted an $8.4 billion oil-production project not in the agreement, which
Seoul has not confirmed.

## Special Briefing No. 5 — One Day, Four Names

- ID: NPSI-20261003-C (as printed on the release) · v1.0.1 · issued 3 October 2026; corrected edition 4 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb5/ · PDF (29 pp., canonical, dark edition): https://npsi.ca/sb5/special-briefing.pdf · cream edition for print: https://npsi.ca/sb5/special-briefing-print.pdf
- Keywords: 15 August 1945, Korea, Japan, 38th parallel, commemoration, official names, liberation, division, Gwangbokjeol, V-J Day, FRUS
- Notes: written in the first person, with passages of opinion marked as such; carries an interest note (the editor's declared Korean-reunification advocacy, https://npsi.ca/disclosure/) and states its AI drafting assistance in the colophon. The page carries the full reading view (ten sections, eleven figures, open items, sources and corrections), ported from the v1.0.1 release on 14 October 2026; the PDF remains the canonical release.

Abstract: The war in the Pacific ended once. It has at least six official
names, and none of them is neutral. Each name is a sentence with a subject
removed, and where the subject went is where the policy lives. Japan's
official name for 15 August, fixed by cabinet decision in 1982, mentions
neither the war's end nor its loss; Seoul's says the light was restored
without naming who restored it; Washington's says victory over Japan, and
Korea is not in the sentence. The briefing reads the names as primary sources
against the documents of 1945, among them Stalin's message of 16 August
accepting the order that split Korea, in which he also asked for the northern
half of Hokkaido, and the three documents behind the legend of the 38th
parallel. It then reads the speeches of 15 August 2026 against the names, and
finds that each did what its name predicted.

Key findings: Japan's official name for the day (Day for Mourning the War Dead
and Praying for Peace, cabinet decision of 13 April 1982) mentions neither the
war's end nor its loss. On 16 August 1945 Stalin accepted the order that split
Korea without mentioning Korea and asked for the northern half of Hokkaido;
Truman declined (FRUS 1945 VI, docs 450, 452). The "two colonels, thirty
minutes, a National Geographic map" story merges three documents carrying two
different dates; Dean Rusk's own account in the government record has no
stopwatch and no map (FRUS 1945 VI, doc 771; Schnabel 1972; Rusk 1990).
Kim Il-sung reached Korea on 19 September 1945, five weeks after liberation;
in 2024, 2025 and 2026 his grandson marked the anniversary with wreaths for
Soviet soldiers. On 15 August 2026 Japan's Emperor spoke of "deep remorse";
the Prime Minister did not use the word, which appears in two of the fifteen
addresses from 2012 to 2026 (2012 and 2025). None of the six official names
says who drew the line across Korea. Germany, through Weizsäcker's address of
8 May 1985, is the control case.

## Special Briefing No. 4 — The Tollgate Markets

- ID: NPSI-20261003-B (as printed on the release) · v1.0.1 · issued 3 October 2026; corrected edition 4 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb4/ · PDF (24 pp., canonical, dark edition): https://npsi.ca/sb4/special-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: market manipulation, securities enforcement, collection rates, investment funds, Turkey, Capital Markets Board, effective repentance, emerging markets, regulatory capacity
- Notes: allegations reported as allegations; no court had ruled on guilt in the Turkish cases as of 4 October 2026. States its AI drafting assistance on the back cover. The page carries the full reading view (eleven sections, fourteen figures, the ladder, the Tollgate Test, the author's signed note, open items, sources and corrections), ported from the v1.0.1 release on 14 October 2026; the PDF remains the canonical release.

Abstract: On 17 September 2026 Turkey's Capital Markets Board ordered 131
investment funds into liquidation in a single day; inside them sat the savings
of 455,758 people. In 2025 the same regulator fined 297 people and companies a
combined TRY 2.69 billion, about 1% of a single money market fund at the
centre of the collapse, and under Article 107(3) of the Capital Markets Law a
person accused of transaction-based manipulation who pays twice the benefit
before an investigation opens faces no penalty at all. The briefing calls such
a place a tollgate market: one where breaking the rules is a toll you pay, not
a wall you hit. It rates seventeen markets on enforcement in practice and
finds that the answer depends less on their laws than on three things the laws
do not show: the gain nobody measures, the fine nobody collects, and the trial
that never comes.

Key findings: When a regulator cannot prove the profit, multiples collapse to
a flat amount (Vietnam: VND 1.5bn, about $57,000, when no gain is
established). From 2007 to 2012 Canada's provincial regulators collected about
35.7% of penalties imposed; British Columbia collected 2.9%. Indonesia's OJK
reported 42 suspected criminal cases under investigation, 32 of them
manipulation, and five concluded cases with final verdicts (9 February 2026).
The markets that most resemble pre-collapse Turkey are Indonesia and Vietnam,
with Thailand close behind and Bangladesh a provisional fourth; severe
sentences arrive after collapses (40 years in Korea, 36 in Singapore, life in
Indonesia). The Tollgate Test: five signs (thin floats and fresh listings;
funds that own each other's trades; "cash" that holds stock; promoters close
to power; a price on prosecution) and four numbers to demand (collection rate,
median fine, referrals and convictions, pay-to-close route).

## Special Briefing No. 3 — The Ledger With One Entry

- ID: NPSI-SB-003 · v1.0.1 (page, 14 October 2026) · PDF v1.0 issued 26 July 2026 (reporting cut-off 22 July 2026); integrated 29 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb3/ · PDF (39 pp., canonical): https://npsi.ca/sb3/special-briefing.pdf
- Companions: WP9 (counterparty reliability), WP1 (diversification thesis), SB1 (jurisdictional exposure)
- Keywords: Venezuela, oil revenue, asset custody, sanctions, escrow, accountability, TRIA, Crystallex, oil-for-food, counterparty risk

Abstract: Since United States forces captured Nicolás Maduro on 3 January 2026,
the American government has controlled the sale of Venezuelan crude oil and the
disposition of its proceeds. The Financial Times estimates those sales have
raised more than US$13 billion; Venezuela's own transparency portal records a
single receipt of $300 million, and no audit has been published. The briefing
verifies the factual record, prices the gap, explains the legal architecture
that produced the offshore structure — two traps in American law that would
have destroyed the funds on arrival — and benchmarks the arrangement against
the three comparable oil-custody regimes of the past quarter-century. It
reaches an uncomfortable conclusion: the Venezuela mechanism is the least
accountable of the four, and the most accountable of them still lost
$8.8 billion.

Key findings: The offshore structure is not evidence of intent to steal — TRIA
§201 attachment and the Crystallex alter-ego doctrine (932 F.3d 126) would
have destroyed the funds on arrival in a U.S. account; the structure built to
defeat Venezuela's creditors also defeats the United States Congress. Four
custody regimes benchmarked (Iraq OFF/DFI, Libya, Iran/Qatar 2023, Venezuela):
Venezuela is the least accountable; Iraq, the most accountable, still lost
$8.8 billion (SIGIR). The intervention redirected rather than interrupted the
oil (1.23m b/d April 2026, highest since 2018); Shandong's independent
refiners were the largest single loser — the Pacific consequence. Every
material claim confidence-rated; both governments flagged as interested
parties; four named unclassified documents would settle the accounting.

## Special Briefing No. 2 — The Three Doors

- ID: NPSI-SB-002 · v1.0.1 · 2 July 2026 · corrected 14 October 2026 (PDF v1.0 canonical)
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb2/ · PDF (canonical): https://npsi.ca/sb2/special-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: critical minerals, Defense Production Act, domestic source, Canada, mining finance, DPA Title III, Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, 42 U.S.C. 18743, EXIM, supply chain

Abstract: Under U.S. defense law, Canada has been a domestic source since 1992
(50 U.S.C. §4552), so Canadian companies apply for Defense Production Act
Title III money on the same footing as a firm in Ohio. This briefing maps that
door and two others that do not depend on it: the Department of Energy's
pilot-project grants under §40210 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
(42 U.S.C. §18743), which require a U.S. site or a U.S. partner that has one,
and the Export-Import Bank's Supply Chain Resiliency Initiative, which finances
foreign projects on the strength of U.S. offtake — and the navigation moat that
stalls applicants.

Key findings: A ten-panel briefing on three doors to U.S. federal money for
Canadian critical-minerals producers. Only Door One, DPA Title III, rests on
the 1992 domestic-source provision (50 U.S.C. §4552), under which Canadian
firms apply on Canadian ground; Door Two, the Department of Energy pilot grants
under §40210 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (42 U.S.C. §18743),
requires a U.S. site or a U.S. partner that has one; Door Three, EXIM's Supply
Chain Resiliency Initiative, finances foreign projects on the strength of
long-term offtake with U.S. buyers. The navigation moat — not eligibility — is
identified as the binding constraint.

## Special Briefing No. 1 — Zero Secrets

- ID: NPSI-SB-001 · v1.0.1 · 11 June 2026 · errata 14 October 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb1/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/sb1/special-briefing.pdf
- Companion: WP5 — Sovereign Compute North (the constructive proposal)
- Keywords: data sovereignty, CLOUD Act, FISA 702, sovereign AI, sovereign compute, cloud jurisdiction, Investment Canada Act, Canada

Abstract: Canada effectively holds no data secrets from the United States — not
by choice, but by architecture. The overwhelming majority of Canadian
government, corporate, and citizen data sits on infrastructure owned by three
American corporations, and under the US CLOUD Act and FISA Section 702,
American jurisdiction follows corporate ownership, not server location. This
briefing audits the exposure, the federal response, and the demonstrated
capability class, and recommends a three-stage sovereign-infrastructure
response.

Key findings: Data residency is not data sovereignty — under the CLOUD Act
(18 U.S.C. §2713) and FISA 702, US jurisdiction follows corporate ownership,
not server location, and no Canada–US CLOUD Act bilateral exists. Anchor
evidence includes Microsoft France's sworn testimony before the French Senate
(10 June 2025). Recommends a control-based definition of sovereign cloud
(jurisdictional, operational, cryptographic, audit), migration of classified
and Protected B workloads, and Canadian-owned-and-operated awards. The caveats
section states the strongest counter-cases (cost, Five Eyes, free-riding)
fairly.

- The Pacific Ledger: https://npsi.ca/ledger/ — the publication's home; current issue and archive.
- Working Papers index: https://npsi.ca/papers/ — every working paper by publication date; the current paper, the archive, the numbering.
- Briefings index: https://npsi.ca/briefings/ — Technical Briefings, Briefing Notes and Special Briefings, by publication date.
- The Number Register: https://npsi.ca/register/ — every identifier the imprint has assigned: publication serials, accession numbers (NPSI-YYYYMMDD-X, assigned at intake, immutable), and reserved numbers never released. Machine-readable: https://npsi.ca/registry.json
- About: https://npsi.ca/about/ — mandate, methodology, editorial standards.
- Disclosure: https://npsi.ca/disclosure/ — declaration of interests: who writes and funds the imprint, every outside interest of the editor's that touches published subject matter, and which papers each interest touches.
- Engage: https://npsi.ca/engage/ — contribution standards for named commentary, corrections, and technical critique.
- Commentary: https://npsi.ca/commentary/ — named commentary: one table of every document open for response.
- Colophon: https://npsi.ca/colophon/ — type, palette, infrastructure.
- Sitemap: https://npsi.ca/sitemap.xml
- Repository: https://github.com/cherishwins/npsi-site — public version-controlled source for the site and papers, with CITATION.cff for academic reuse.
